paragraphs.text: Lesson 13, a complicated coffee order.
Lisa works at a coffee shop, and Andy comes in to make his order, but there are a few problems.
Listen to their conversation and mark these statements true or false.
Hi, what can I get for you today?
Hi there. I'll have a double mint chocolate espresso with just a hint of cinnamon and a dash of whipped cream.
I'm sorry, but we don't do customized drinks. If you want, I can make you a regular espresso.
I don't want a regular espresso. I want a double mint chocolate espresso with just a hint of cinnamon and a dash of whipped cream.
It's not rocket science. You did graduate from high school, didn't you?
I'm actually in college. I work here part-time. It helps me pay for my books.
Then you can surely figure out how to make my order the way I want. It's a double mint chocolate espresso with a bit of cinnamon and a dash of whipped cream.
Sir, the coffee cup only prepares drinks listed on the menu. It's written right over there.
Doesn't your menu offer drinks with mint chocolate ingredients?
Well, yes. There's our mint chocolate iced latte. Would you like one of those?
No. Just add the mint chocolate stuff to my espresso. I'll pay the higher price for the latte.
I'm not asking you to break the law here. Just bend the rules a little bit. After all, I'm a regular.
Look, I'm new here. This is my fourth day on the job. And today my manager left me alone for the first time.
Now, I'll make you any drink listed on the menu. If you want to wait until my manager gets back from the bank,
then you can take it up with her. I'll only make you a customized drink if she gives the green light.
Alright, never mind. Just make me a white chocolate cappuccino with almond milk then.
We only have regular milk and soy milk, sir.
What kind of coffee shop doesn't carry almond milk? How about if I buy my own almond milk at the store across the street and give it to you,
then you could make my cappuccino?
Sir, I'm sorry, but I'm not allowed to make any drink that is not listed on the menu. That's the policy and my hands are tied.
Good grief! Whatever happened to the customer is always right!
Ugh, okay. Can you make me a double peanut butter fudge espresso? That drink is clearly listed on the menu.
We're out of fudge, sir. I'm sorry. Is there another drink you would like to order?
How can I, when you refuse to make any of my favorite drinks and you're out of half the ingredients? Fine.
Umm... Just make me a raspberry espresso.
I can do that! Wait. No, I can't. I just remembered something.
What is it now? Our espresso machine is out of order. Can I offer you a regular cup of coffee instead?
We also have an excellent selection of herbal teas. Just give me a plain black cup of coffee and let me get out of here!
Coming right up. Now let's learn the vocabulary from this dialogue. Andy asks for a double mint chocolate espresso with just a hint of cinnamon and a dash of whipped cream.
The words hint and dash both mean a very small amount. Unfortunately, Lisa says that the cafe doesn't make customized drinks, and Andy gets a little bit annoyed.
He says it's not rocket science. This means it's not complicated or it's not difficult to make the drink he wants.
He says, you can surely figure out how to make my order the way I want. The phrasal verb figure out can mean discover or understand.
One of the drinks served at the cafe is a mint chocolate iced latte. The word latte refers to a drink that's espresso coffee with steamed milk.
That means the milk is hot. It's heated up. Although in the case of this latte, it's an iced latte meaning the drink is cold.

But Andy doesn't want this drink. He says, no, just add the mint chocolate stuff to my espresso. The word stuff is a general word for material or items, and the word stuff is uncountable, so there's no such word as stuffs. It's always stuff.
Andy says, I'm not asking you to break the law here. Just bend the rules a little bit.
Bend the rules means allow something that is not normally permitted. Then he says, after all, I'm a regular. After all means after everything else has been considered.
And the expression, I'm a regular means I'm a frequent customer who always comes to this cafe. But Lisa refuses to make an exception.

She says, if you want to wait until my manager gets back from the bank, then you can take it up with her. This expression, take it up with her, means start the discussion with her, or make the complaint to her.
Lisa says, I'll only make you a customized drink if she gives the green light. The expression gives the green light means gives approval.
So Andy says, alright, never mind. Just make me a white chocolate cappuccino with almond milk then.
And almond is a type of nut. Almond milk is a drink that's similar to milk, but it's made from nuts and not from animal products, so almond milk is appropriate for vegetarians.
But Lisa says, we only have regular milk and soy milk. Soy is a type of bean, soy milk is also a vegetarian type of milk.

Andy is surprised and upset and he insists on getting a customized drink. But Lisa stands firm. She says, I'm not allowed to make any drink that is not listed on the menu. That's the policy and my hands are tied.
This expression, my hands are tied, means I have no power or no ability or authority to do it.

So finally Andy asks for a drink that's on the menu, a double peanut butter fudge espresso. The word fudge refers to a soft candy that's made of sugar, milk, butter, and flavors. Fudge is often chocolate flavored.
But Lisa says, we're out of fudge sir, I'm sorry. We're out of means we don't have anymore.

In response, Andy asks for a simple raspberry espresso and Lisa says she can make it, but then she realizes she can't because the espresso machine is out of order. If a machine is out of order, it means it's not functioning. It's broken. It's not working.
So finally, Andy says, just give me a plain black cup of coffee and let me get out of here. He uses a couple of expressions that are reductions.
Gimme, gimme means give me. But in fast spoken English, the words give me tend to run together, gimme. And get out of here.
Outa means out of, but again in fast spoken English it sounds like outa. What does Andy want? A plain black cup of coffee. The word plain means regular, normal, without anything special added.
And Lisa says coming right up. This is a phrase that waiters, waitresses, and other servers used to say your order will be ready very soon.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation. Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice and the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
